verses.text: It was the fifteenth year of the reign of Emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea. Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip was tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis—far to the north, at the edge of the known world, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene—another remote province.

footnotes.content: Tiberius Claudius Nero ruled the Roman Empire from AD 14-37. Known for his ruthlessness, he was already being worshipped as a god in parts of the empire. While the "divine" emperor sat on his throne in Rome, the true God sent his message to a nameless man in the wilderness.

Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26-36. He ruled the region with an iron fist. Years later, he will sentence Jesus to death. Here he is just one political figure among many—still unaware of the role he will play.
Son of Herod the Great, he ruled as tetrarch over Galilee and Perea. Not a king, but a vassal of Rome—a ruler "by Rome's permission." He will later have John executed.

verses.text:
Annas and Caiaphas were high priests—so many rulers, secular and religious, all claiming authority.

And then it happened: The word of God came to John, son of Zechariah. In the wilderness—far from temples and palaces, in the very place where Israel had once been formed.

footnotes.content: There was supposed to be only one high priest. Annas had served from AD 6-15 and was deposed by Rome, but retained great influence. His son-in-law Caiaphas was the sitting high priest (AD 18-36). The dual naming reflects the complicated power dynamics under Roman rule.

The classic prophetic commissioning formula (cf. Jer 1:1; Ezek 1:3). Luke deliberately places John in the line of Israel's great prophets. After centuries of prophetic silence—God speaks again. Not to the powerful in Rome or Jerusalem, but to a hermit in the wilderness.

verses.text: John went through the entire Jordan region, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

footnotes.content: Not merely a washing, but a sign of radical life change. "Repentance" (μετάνοια) literally means "a change of mind"—a complete reorientation of life. "For the forgiveness of sins" does not mean the baptism automatically forgives, but that it opens the way to forgiveness.

verses.text: As it is written in the book of the words of the prophet Isaiah:"A voice cries out in the wilderness:Prepare the way of the Lord!Make his paths straight!

footnotes.content: The longest Isaiah quotation in all of Luke-Acts—a sign of its programmatic importance. Luke quotes further than Matthew and Mark, all the way to "all flesh shall see God's salvation" (v.6). This universal perspective is central to Luke: God's rescue is not for Israel alone, but for the whole world.

lines.text: "A voice cries out in the wilderness:
Prepare the way of the Lord!

verses.text: Every valley shall be filled in,every mountain and hill brought low.The crooked shall become straight,the rough ways made smooth.

lines.text: Every valley shall be filled in,
every mountain and hill brought low.

verses.text: And all flesh shall see God's salvation—all people, everywhere."

lines.text: And all flesh shall see God's salvation—all people, everywhere."

sections.heading: Brood of Vipers Before the Fire

verses.text:
Crowds streamed out to be baptized by him. But John didn't mince words:

"You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

footnotes.content: A shocking image, echoing the serpent from Genesis 3. Not: "You are like snakes," but: "You are children of the ancient serpent." Prophetic sharpness meant to shake people awake—not a polite invitation, but an alarm.

verses.text: Produce fruit—real fruit that shows you're serious about repentance! And don't start telling yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' I tell you, God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones!

footnotes.content: Many believed that belonging to Abraham's lineage guaranteed salvation. John shatters this illusion: ancestry alone does not save. God can raise up children of Abraham from these stones—he doesn't depend on biological descendants.

verses.text: The axe is already at the root of the trees—judgment is not someday, it is now. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire."
The crowd asked him, "What then should we do?"
John answered, "Anyone who has two shirts should share with someone who has none. And anyone who has food should do the same."

footnotes.content: Concrete ethics, not abstract theology. Repentance shows itself not in pious words but in sharing with the poor. This instruction is aimed at ordinary people—no heroic sacrifices demanded, just practical solidarity.

verses.text: Even tax collectors came to be baptized. They asked him, "Teacher, what should we do?"

footnotes.content: Not the wealthy chief tax collectors, but local revenue agents who worked for Rome. They were seen as collaborators with the occupying power and were socially despised—routinely assumed to be cheats. That they came to John was remarkable.

verses.text: He said, "Collect no more than what is prescribed—be honest, even when no one is watching."

Soldiers also asked him, "And what about us—what should we do?"

He answered, "Don't extort anyone, don't make false accusations, and be content with your wages—don't use your power to enrich yourselves."

footnotes.content: Probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas, not Roman legionaries. They had power over ordinary people and could easily abuse it—through extortion, false accusations, or violence.

verses.text: The people were filled with expectation. Everyone was quietly wondering whether John himself might be the Messiah.

footnotes.content: "The Anointed One"—the king promised by God who would liberate Israel and bring justice. Under Roman occupation, the longing for the Messiah was especially intense. John was a fascinating figure—no wonder people asked if he might be the one.

verses.text:
John answered them all:

"I baptize you with water. But one who is mightier than I is coming. I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals—I am not even the least servant in his household. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.

footnotes.content: In the Old Testament, God himself is often called "the Mighty One of Israel." The historical John probably expected God's direct intervention. Christians saw this expectation fulfilled in Jesus.
The lowest slave's task. Even disciples were not expected to remove their teacher's sandals. John places himself below the lowest slave—so great is the distance between him and the Coming One.

Fire carries a double meaning: purification (like silver refined in a crucible) and judgment (like chaff burned). Pentecost will fulfill this promise, when the Spirit descends in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). Luke connects John's announcement with the Pentecost experience.

verses.text: He has his winnowing fork in hand—the farmer's tool at harvest time. He will thoroughly clean out his threshing floor, gathering the wheat into his barn but burning the chaff with unquenchable fire—judgment is coming, and there is no escape."

footnotes.content: On the threshing floor, threshed grain was thrown into the air. The wind separated the light chaff from the heavy grain. The chaff was burned, the grain stored in the barn. An image of final judgment: separation and decision.

verses.text: With many other exhortations, he proclaimed good news to the people. Yes, good news—because even the warning about fire was a call to rescue.

footnotes.content: Remarkably, Luke calls John's judgment preaching "good news" (gospel). Warning of judgment and invitation to rescue belong together. The message is serious, but its goal is repentance and salvation—not condemnation.

verses.text: But Herod the tetrarch—whom John had publicly rebuked about Herodias, his brother's wife, and about all the other evil things Herod had done—

footnotes.content: She had divorced her husband Philip and married his half-brother Antipas—while Philip was still alive. By Jewish law this was both incest (marrying a sister-in-law, Lev 18:16) and adultery. John called things by their proper names.

verses.text: added this to everything else: He locked John up in prison. The prophetic voice was silenced—at least for now.
When all the people were being baptized—one after another, a stream of people wanting to turn their lives around, Jesus too was baptized. And while he was praying, heaven was opened,

footnotes.content: Only Luke mentions that Jesus was praying during his baptism. In his Gospel, Jesus prays before all important moments: before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the Transfiguration (9:28-29), in Gethsemane (22:41-44). Prayer opens heaven.
An apocalyptic motif—the barrier between God's world and the earthly world is broken through. Isaiah 64:1 had longed: "Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down!" Here it happens.

verses.text:
and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven:

"You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased—completely pleased, from the very beginning."

footnotes.content: Luke emphasizes this was not an inner experience but a visible manifestation. The Spirit manifests physically, tangibly—God acts in the material world.
The dove recalls the creation story (the Spirit hovering over the waters) and Noah's ark (the dove signaling the flood's end). New beginning. New creation. Jesus' baptism inaugurates a new era.

A "heavenly voice" (Hebrew: bat qol) was considered in Judaism as a form of divine communication after the end of prophecy. Hard for some listeners today to imagine—was it an audible phenomenon? An inner certainty? The text describes it as a real event that publicly confirms Jesus' unique relationship with God.

The heavenly voice weaves together three Old Testament texts: (1) Psalm 2:7—royal enthronement ("You are my Son"), (2) Genesis 22:2—Isaac as "beloved son" (sacrifice motif), (3) Isaiah 42:1—the suffering Servant. Jesus is simultaneously King, Sacrifice, and Servant. His identity already contains his path.

sections.heading: Genealogy: From Son of God to Son of God

verses.text:
Jesus was about thirty years old when he began his ministry. He was known as the son of Joseph—at least that was the common assumption.

Joseph was son of Heli,

footnotes.content: The age at which David became king (2 Sam 5:4), Joseph entered Pharaoh's service in Egypt (Gen 41:46), and Levites began their temple service (Num 4:3). An age for public ministry, for maturity in calling.
Luke maintains the virgin birth while documenting the legal lineage through Joseph. "He was known as"—socially and legally Joseph was his father, but Luke knows the deeper truth.

verses.text: Heli son of Matthat, Matthat son of Levi, Levi son of Melchi, Melchi son of Jannai, Jannai son of Joseph,
Joseph son of Mattathias, Mattathias son of Amos, Amos son of Nahum, Nahum son of Esli, Esli son of Naggai,
Naggai son of Maath, Maath son of Mattathias, Mattathias son of Semein, Semein son of Josech, Josech son of Joda,
Joda son of Joanan, Joanan son of Rhesa, Rhesa son of Zerubbabel, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Shealtiel son of Neri,

footnotes.content: A descendant of David who led the people back after the Babylonian exile and rebuilt the temple (Ezra 3:2; Hag 1:1). A bearer of hope in a dark time.

verses.text: Neri son of Melchi, Melchi son of Addi, Addi son of Cosam, Cosam son of Elmadam, Elmadam son of Er,
Er son of Joshua, Joshua son of Eliezer, Eliezer son of Jorim, Jorim son of Matthat, Matthat son of Levi,
Levi son of Simeon, Simeon son of Judah, Judah son of Joseph, Joseph son of Jonam, Jonam son of Eliakim,
Eliakim son of Melea, Melea son of Menna, Menna son of Mattatha, Mattatha son of Nathan, Nathan son of David,

footnotes.content: Luke traces the line through Nathan, another son of David, while Matthew goes through Solomon. Different traditions, different theological emphases. The differences cannot be fully harmonized, but both testify: Jesus descends from the house of David.

verses.text: David son of Jesse, Jesse son of Obed, Obed son of Boaz, Boaz son of Salmon, Salmon son of Nahshon,
Nahshon son of Amminadab, Amminadab son of Admin, Admin son of Arni, Arni son of Hezron, Hezron son of Perez, Perez son of Judah,
Judah son of Jacob, Jacob son of Isaac, Isaac son of Abraham, Abraham son of Terah, Terah son of Nahor,

footnotes.content: At this point Matthew's genealogy ends. Luke continues—beyond Israel's borders to all of humanity. Jesus is not only Israel's Messiah but the Savior of the world.

verses.text: Nahor son of Serug, Serug son of Reu, Reu son of Peleg, Peleg son of Eber, Eber son of Shelah,
Shelah son of Cainan, Cainan son of Arphaxad, Arphaxad son of Shem, Shem son of Noah, Noah son of Lamech,

footnotes.content: The line reaches back beyond the flood—to a time before humanity was divided into nations. Noah was the ancestor of all people after the flood.

verses.text: Lamech son of Methuselah, Methuselah son of Enoch, Enoch son of Jared, Jared son of Mahalalel, Mahalalel son of Cainan,

Cainan son of Enosh, Enosh son of Seth, Seth son of Adam.

Adam—the first human was son of God. And Jesus is so even more.

footnotes.content: The first human. Luke traces the line to the beginning of humanity. Jesus belongs not only to one nation but to the entire human family. What was broken in Adam is being restored in Jesus.

A unique conclusion for an ancient genealogy. Adam was created by God (Gen 2:7), and is in that sense "son of God." But the genealogy runs from Jesus to Adam to God—and the heavenly voice has just called Jesus "my beloved Son." The arc closes: Jesus is Son of God in a deeper sense than Adam ever was.
